body: Where Insomniac’s Spider-man was an open world feast, their take on Marvel’s Wolverine is more along the lines of a cinematic summer blockbuster

It is only natural to expect a large, open world game featuring everyone’s favourite X-Man, Wolverine. Given Insomniac Games’ track record of making three excellent Spider-man open world games, Wolverine is quite different. It is a bloody, visceral, action-packed rollercoaster ride akin to Call of Duty . So, before going in, it is important to temper your expectations and that is where Wolverine is at its most enjoyable.

Completely sidestepping the normal X-Men timelines, Wolverine is set in its own alternate reality and follows the shadowy Team X. Comprising mutant operatives Sabretooth and Mystique, this version of the black-ops team is led by Dr. Nathanial Essex, who comic fans will recognise as Mr. Sinister. There is no Magneto or Professor X here, instead mutants are being actively hunted by Bolivar Trask, for his infernal experiments.

Freed from the shackles of being tied to the movies or past games, Wolverine powers through with its own world and narrative. Logan, aka Wolverine, is excellently portrayed, from his wild man origins to an angry hero who clearly hides a lot of pain behind his expressive eyes as he slashes through the story with blind ferocity.

Also read: Here’s a bunch of video games that let you be a superhero

This narrative is a big, fat, bloody, adamantium clad freight train that is on the rails, even while it feels a bit restrictive, as you are led by the hand from one section to another, with cutscenes in the middle. It almost feels like the first God of War games, but this is slightly more committed to its linearity.

Wolverine ’s combat system is fast and furious, blending the tried and tested Spiderman formula, with a healthy dash of a Sekiro -like parry system. Though, the parries are more stylish and cinematically handled, and in many fights with other famous villains from the X-Men universe, it has Wolverine duck, roll and parry to survive. Successful parries not only reward you with free hits, but also feel excellent.

headline: What are the AI threats flagged by Anthropic? | Explained
body: Anthropic released information about several malicious activities detected and disrupted between December 2025 and August 2026, which had serious implications across seven key areas: scams and fraud, cyber operations, illicit distillation, influence operations, surveillance operations, conventional weapons and biological misuse

Amid heightened debates about threats from and responsible use of artificial intelligence, Anthropic, the research-based U.S. company behind the Claude family of large language models and other AI products, has released several cases of misuse of its systems, warning of growing risks as AI models become more capable.

In a 154-page report published on Thursday (September 10, 2026), the firm released information about several malicious activities detected and disrupted between December 2025 and August 2026, which had serious implications across seven key areas: scams and fraud, cyber operations, illicit distillation, influence operations, surveillance operations, conventional weapons and biological misuse. The actors behind the detected misuse included suspected state-sponsored groups, financially motivated criminals, state propaganda institutions and politically motivated individuals.

While the capabilities of AI systems to target cyber operations, spread misinformation, and enable surveillance have been discussed since their inception, the scope of biological misuse is a relatively new development. In the report titled “Detecting and countering misuse of AI”, Anthropic referred to biological misuse as “one of the most serious risks” of frontier AI, which could have “catastrophic consequences” without the correct safeguards.

The report, coincidentally, comes a day after Jacob Coxon , an AI researcher at Anthropic, quit his post, saying that AI companies were “gambling with our lives” and that the people building AI “earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade”.

Anthropic, in the report, furnished examples of the most notable and novel malicious activities, ranging from fake dating apps designed to defraud users to sophisticated surveillance systems designed to monitor dissidents, identified and disrupted by its “Threat Intelligence” team.

A majority of the operations mentioned in the report, Anthropic said, were directly executed or orchestrated by AI. The use of AI involved multi-agent frameworks for reconnaissance, data filtration, and exploitation instead of simple questions and responses from chatbots. Humans were involved in setting up targets and reviewing exfiltration, it said.

headline: Apple’s ‘Surprise and Shine’ event: What to expect from John Ternus’s first keynote on September 9
body: This is John Ternus’s first opportunity to set a tone as CEO by showing whether Apple under his watch will keep leaning on operational discipline, or push harder into new categories
full_body:

On September 9, Apple starts a new chapter. The “Surprise and Shine” event at the Steve Jobs Theatre in Cupertino will be the first product launch under CEO John Ternus, who formally took over from Tim Cook on September 1. As someone who has been building Apple’s hardware for over two decades, from the Cinema Display to the iPhone Air, Mr. Ternus is expected to unveil the $4.6 trillion company’s first foldable iPhone.

It is widely speculated that the first foldable iPhone would be called “ultra”, and that it would be Apple’s biggest form-factor shift since the iPhone X ditched the home button in 2017. Given Mr. Ternus’s track record of coordinating hardware and silicon teams, as seen with the iPhone Air’s tightly integrated chassis, chip, and modem, expect the foldable to lean heavily on custom engineering rather than a straightforward hinge-and-glass exercise.

Alongside the fold, Apple is expected to unveil the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max. These are two time-tested variants in the iPhone line-up and so expect design continuity rather than reinvention with some minor changes like a smaller Dynamic Island. Separately, the standard iPhone 18 and iPhone Air’s next generation may get pushed to spring 2027, suggesting Apple may be splitting its iPhone cycle for the first time in years. This would mean premium hardware in September, and affordable models later.

Expect updated Apple Watch Series 12 and Watch Ultra 4 models, and possibly a refreshed AirPods lineup. The bigger surprise could be on the smart-home front as rumours point to a long-awaited home hub device, a new Apple TV 4K, and an updated HomePod mini. These are products Mr. Ternus is believed to be personally keen on expanding as he looks to build product lines beyond the iPhone, much like what he did with AirPods and the iPad earlier in his career.

Don’t expect deep dives into Apple Intelligence or Siri here as this event is traditionally about hardware and release windows. Apple is likely to confirm launch dates for iOS 27, iPadOS 27, and macOS Golden Gate, but the harder questions about Apple’s AI strategy will probably wait for another day.

This is Mr. Ternus’s first opportunity to set a tone as CEO by showing whether Apple under his watch will keep leaning on operational discipline the way it did under Mr. Cook, or just push harder into new categories the way his own career suggests he might.

full_body:
The BSE Sensex fell 116.82 points, or 0.15%, to 76,398.61 at 9:21 am. The Nifty 50 declined 44.65 points, or 0.19%, to 23,853.05.

Oil prices extended gains on Monday as tit-for-tat strikes between the US and Iran on vessels sailing in the Strait of Hormuz and other areas heightened concerns over prolonged supply disruptions from the Middle East.

Brent crude futures rose 52 cents, or 0.54%, to $96.80 a barrel by 2354 GMT, while US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude gained 66 cents, or 0.72%, to $92.14 a barrel.

Asian shares rallied on Monday as a robust US jobs report boosted optimism over global economic growth, even as it reduced expectations of an interest-rate cut. Oil prices edged higher after the US and Iran attacked ships in the Gulf.

Japan’s Nikkei 225 rebounded 2%, recovering after a similar decline last week, while South Korea’s Kospi surged 3%. MSCI’s broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan gained 0.9%.

Developments in the West Asia conflict, crude oil prices and US inflation data are expected to be the key factors driving the stock market next week, analysts said. Foreign investor activity and global market trends will also influence domestic equities. “The week ahead is likely to remain highly sensitive to global monetary policy, crude oil prices and geopolitical developments,” said Ajit Mishra, SVP, Research, Religare Broking Ltd told PTI.

Investors will closely track the impact of stronger-than-expected US employment data on expectations for the Federal Reserve’s September policy decision, Mishra said. On the domestic front, market participants will monitor foreign institutional flows, the rupee, crude oil prices and domestic liquidity.

“Developments around the Strait of Hormuz will also remain a critical monitorable given their implications for India’s inflation, external balance and corporate profitability,” Mishra added.
